message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"45e1187eb0bf1931a96c63480ce8c738d99ab5bb542c8baad3acd8ad9bae6201","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-sc-class-d:lineage:71","source_registry_sha256":"61c32f86a25e3c021742b3c9ddf64a97709817dd75a19df6d2b69eac0a40c4f1","units":[{"unit_id":"sec07-u01","module_id":"sec07-m01","objective_ids":["sec07-u01"],"title":{"text":"Yielding the right-of-way","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Right-of-way rules decide who goes first, and misreading them causes many intersection crashes.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F04","sec07-F06"]},{"text":"No driver is ever automatically owed the right-of-way, so judgment always matters.","fact_ids":["sec07-F02"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Sam and another driver reach a four-way stop at the same moment, and the other driver is on Sam's right.","fact_ids":["sec07-F06"]},"reasoning":{"text":"When two drivers arrive together at a stop-sign-controlled four-way intersection, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right.","fact_ids":["sec07-R01","sec07-F06"]},"result":{"text":"Sam waits for the driver on the right to go first, then proceeds after checking the intersection is clear.","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-F03"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking the driver on the right always goes first at any intersection.","fact_ids":["sec07-R01","sec07-F04"]},"correction":{"text":"The Same Time Rule applies only when both arrive together; otherwise the first car to arrive goes first.","fact_ids":["sec07-R01","sec07-F04"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"First there goes first; on a tie, the right goes first; left turns and joining drivers give way.","fact_ids":["sec07-F04","sec07-F06","sec07-F05","sec07-R02"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"At a stop-sign-controlled four-way intersection, two drivers arrive together. Who goes first?","fact_ids":["sec07-F06"]},"answer":{"text":"The driver on the right.","fact_ids":["sec07-F06"]},"rationale":{"text":"The Same Time Rule gives priority to the driver on the right when arrival is simultaneous.","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-R01"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Who goes first?","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F04","sec07-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Rules for yielding","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F04","sec07-F06"]},{"text":"Judgment still matters","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F04","sec07-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Right-of-way rules tell drivers who should yield and in what order to enter and drive through an intersection or a similar situation when other drivers or pedestrians are present. But the rules are a guide, not a guarantee. Nobody should assume the right-of-way is automatically theirs, because the situation and circumstances at each intersection always have to be considered. In this unit you will learn the main yielding rules in the manual, including the First Car Rule and the Same Time Rule, and the rules for left turns and entering roads.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F04","sec07-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Yield to those already there","fact_ids":["sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pedestrians, bicyclists, drivers in the intersection","fact_ids":["sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},{"text":"First Car Rule: earlier arrival goes first","fact_ids":["sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Yield to pedestrians, bicyclists and other drivers who are still in the intersection, even if your light has just turned green. Then apply arrival order: yield to a driver who is already at the intersection or arrives there before you. The manual illustrates this as the First Car Rule. Whoever arrives first gets to go first, as long as the way is clear. This simple rule settles most stop sign intersections, and it works because every driver can see who stopped first and can take turns in order. Clear, predictable choices at intersections keep everyone moving safely.","fact_ids":["sec07-F03","sec07-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The Same Time Rule","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Four-way stop, same arrival","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-R01"]},{"text":"Yield to the driver on your right","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"At a four-way intersection controlled by stop signs, if you and another driver arrive at the same time, yield to the driver on your right. The manual calls this the Same Time Rule. It only applies when both drivers reach the intersection together; then the driver on the left gives way to the driver on the right. If one driver clearly arrived first, the First Car Rule applies instead. So the first question at a four-way stop is who arrived first, and only a tie brings the Same Time Rule into play. When in doubt, waiting a moment longer is always the safer choice.","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"The always-right myth","fact_ids":["sec07-R01","sec07-F04","sec07-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Myth: the right always goes first","fact_ids":["sec07-R01","sec07-F04","sec07-F02"]},{"text":"Truth: only on a tie","fact_ids":["sec07-R01","sec07-F04","sec07-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a common misconception: the driver on the right always has the right-of-way. That is only true at a four-way stop when both drivers arrive at the same time. When one driver arrives first, the First Car Rule gives that driver the right to go first, wherever the other car is. And even then, no one should assume the right-of-way is automatically theirs. Watch the other driver, make eye contact if you can, and be ready to wait if someone does not follow the rules. Making eye contact with other drivers helps confirm who is going. These rules work only when every driver follows them.","fact_ids":["sec07-R01","sec07-F04","sec07-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Turning left and joining traffic","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F08","sec07-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Left turns yield to oncoming traffic","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F08","sec07-R02"]},{"text":"Driveways and private roads yield","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F08","sec07-R02"]},{"text":"Ramps yield to highway traffic","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F08","sec07-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"When you are making a left turn, yield to drivers in the opposing traffic lane. When you enter a public highway from a driveway or a private road, yield to the drivers already on that highway. On an entrance or acceleration ramp, yield to drivers who are already on the limited access or interstate highway. The common thread is simple: turning left, you give way to oncoming drivers, and joining a road, you give way to the drivers already on it. Wait for a safe gap rather than forcing others to make room for you. Patience at intersections prevents many of the most common crashes.","fact_ids":["sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F08","sec07-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Quick right-of-way check","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-R01","sec07-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Four-way stop, same arrival","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-R01","sec07-F04"]},{"text":"Who goes first?","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-R01","sec07-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you and another driver arrive at a four-way stop at exactly the same time, and the other driver is on your right. Who goes first? The answer is the driver on your right. Under the Same Time Rule, when both drivers arrive together at a stop-sign-controlled four-way intersection, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right. If one of you had clearly arrived first, the First Car Rule would let that driver go first instead, as long as the way is clear. Yielding is a courtesy and a safety habit, not a sign of weakness.","fact_ids":["sec07-F06","sec07-R01","sec07-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Right-of-way recap","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F03","sec07-F04","sec07-F06","sec07-R01","sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F08","sec07-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Never assume it","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F03","sec07-F04","sec07-F06","sec07-R01","sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F08","sec07-R02"]},{"text":"First car first, tie goes right","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F03","sec07-F04","sec07-F06","sec07-R01","sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F08","sec07-R02"]},{"text":"Left turns and joiners give way","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F03","sec07-F04","sec07-F06","sec07-R01","sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F08","sec07-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close, right-of-way rules decide who yields and in what order, but no one should assume the right-of-way is automatically theirs. Yield to anyone still in the intersection. The first driver to arrive goes first, and when two drivers arrive together at a four-way stop, the driver on the right goes first. When turning left, yield to oncoming traffic, and when entering a road from a driveway, a private road or a ramp, yield to drivers already on it. Wait for a safe gap and stay ready for others' mistakes. Watch for drivers who may not follow the rules.","fact_ids":["sec07-F01","sec07-F02","sec07-F03","sec07-F04","sec07-F06","sec07-R01","sec07-F05","sec07-F07","sec07-F08","sec07-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec07-u02","module_id":"sec07-m02","objective_ids":["sec07-u02"],"title":{"text":"Traffic signals","fact_ids":["sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-F11"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Each signal light carries a specific instruction, and confusing steady and flashing lights is a common error.","fact_ids":["sec07-F13","sec07-F18","sec07-F19"]},{"text":"Right turn on red is allowed only with the correct stop and yield.","fact_ids":["sec07-F16","sec07-F17"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Lee approaches an intersection where the yellow light is flashing, not steady.","fact_ids":["sec07-F18"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A flashing yellow means slow down and proceed with caution, ready to stop for traffic entering the intersection.","fact_ids":["sec07-F18","sec07-R04"]},"result":{"text":"Lee slows, scans for cross traffic and continues through carefully without stopping, since nothing is entering.","fact_ids":["sec07-F18"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a flashing red light means wait until it turns green.","fact_ids":["sec07-R06"]},"correction":{"text":"A flashing red works like a stop sign: stop completely, look both ways, yield if needed and then go.","fact_ids":["sec07-F19","sec07-R06"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Steady yellow, stop and wait; flashing yellow, slow and careful; flashing red, stop sign rules.","fact_ids":["sec07-F13","sec07-F18","sec07-F19"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"What must you do at a steady red light before turning right, where turning on red is allowed?","fact_ids":["sec07-F17"]},"answer":{"text":"Stop before the near-side crosswalk and yield to pedestrians and other lawful traffic.","fact_ids":["sec07-F17"]},"rationale":{"text":"Right on red always begins with a full stop before the crosswalk and yielding.","fact_ids":["sec07-F17","sec07-F16"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Reading traffic signals","fact_ids":["sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-F12","sec07-F18","sec07-F19"]},"lines":[{"text":"Signals tell you when to stop and go","fact_ids":["sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-F12","sec07-F18","sec07-F19"]},{"text":"Steady and flashing lights differ","fact_ids":["sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-F12","sec07-F18","sec07-F19"]}],"narration":{"text":"Traffic control devices include traffic signals, signs and pavement markings, plus directions given by law enforcement, highway personnel and school crossing guards. Traffic signals are lights that tell you when or where to stop and go, and they are usually found at intersections. In this unit you will learn the order of the lights, what each steady light means, what to do when a light changes, how to turn right on red, and what flashing yellow and flashing red lights require. Steady and flashing lights mean different things, so learn them as pairs.","fact_ids":["sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-F12","sec07-F18","sec07-F19"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"How signals are arranged","fact_ids":["sec07-F10","sec07-F11","sec07-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Vertical: red top, green bottom","fact_ids":["sec07-F10","sec07-F11","sec07-R03"]},{"text":"Horizontal: red left, green right","fact_ids":["sec07-F10","sec07-F11","sec07-R03"]},{"text":"Some show one color only","fact_ids":["sec07-F10","sec07-F11","sec07-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"On a single vertical signal, red is at the top, yellow in the middle and green at the bottom. Some metropolitan areas use horizontal signals instead, with the red light on the left, yellow in the middle and green on the right. Some intersections and other locations have signals with lights of only one color, either green, yellow or red. Knowing the arrangement helps you read a signal quickly, for example when glare makes it hard to tell which light is lit, because the position tells you the color. Reading the signal correctly is the first step in every intersection decision.","fact_ids":["sec07-F10","sec07-F11","sec07-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Green and steady yellow","fact_ids":["sec07-F12","sec07-F13","sec07-F14","sec07-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Green: go with caution if clear","fact_ids":["sec07-F12","sec07-F13","sec07-F14","sec07-R05"]},{"text":"Steady yellow: stop and wait","fact_ids":["sec07-F12","sec07-F13","sec07-F14","sec07-R05"]},{"text":"Already in the intersection: clear it","fact_ids":["sec07-F12","sec07-F13","sec07-F14","sec07-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"A green light means you may go through the intersection with caution if it is clear to do so. A steady yellow light follows the green and warns that the signal is about to turn red, so you should stop and wait for the next green. If you are already inside the intersection when the light turns yellow, clear it as quickly as you can. As you approach a yellow light, watch for and allow for mistakes by other drivers beside, ahead of and behind you, since not everyone will react the same way. Always look for cross traffic, even when your signal says go.","fact_ids":["sec07-F12","sec07-F13","sec07-F14","sec07-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Steady red and right on red","fact_ids":["sec07-F15","sec07-F16","sec07-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"Red: stop and wait for green","fact_ids":["sec07-F15","sec07-F16","sec07-F17"]},{"text":"Right on red unless a sign forbids","fact_ids":["sec07-F15","sec07-F16","sec07-F17"]},{"text":"Stop before the crosswalk, then yield","fact_ids":["sec07-F15","sec07-F16","sec07-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"A red light means stop before entering the intersection and wait behind the stop line, crosswalk or intersection until the light turns green. Traffic facing a red signal may turn right, except where a sign prohibits a right turn on red. To turn right on red, stop before the crosswalk on the near side of the turn and yield to pedestrians lawfully in or next to it and to other traffic lawfully using the intersection. A right on red is never a rolling turn; it always starts with a complete stop. Signals guide traffic, but your own judgment still matters.","fact_ids":["sec07-F15","sec07-F16","sec07-F17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Steady versus flashing yellow","fact_ids":["sec07-R04","sec07-F13","sec07-F18"]},"lines":[{"text":"Steady yellow: stop and wait","fact_ids":["sec07-R04","sec07-F13","sec07-F18"]},{"text":"Flashing yellow: proceed with caution","fact_ids":["sec07-R04","sec07-F13","sec07-F18"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap. Drivers often treat every yellow light the same way. A steady yellow tells you to stop and wait for the next green, while a flashing yellow lets you keep going slowly with caution, ready to stop for entering traffic. A flashing yellow means slow down and go ahead with caution, ready to stop for any traffic that may be entering the intersection. Mixing them up leads either to unnecessary stops or, worse, to rolling through a steady yellow that is about to turn red. Take the color and the flashing pattern into account together.","fact_ids":["sec07-R04","sec07-F13","sec07-F18"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Flashing red","fact_ids":["sec07-F19","sec07-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Treat it like a stop sign","fact_ids":["sec07-F19","sec07-R06"]},{"text":"Full stop, look, yield, then go","fact_ids":["sec07-F19","sec07-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"At a flashing red light you come to a complete stop behind the stop line, crosswalk or intersection, just as you would at a stop sign. Then look both ways and yield if required before entering. After that complete stop, you may enter once you have looked both ways and yielded where needed. That is the stop sign procedure, rather than a wait for green. A flashing red often appears when a signal is operating in a special mode, so treat it with the same care you give any stop sign. A complete stop is never wasted when the rule calls for one.","fact_ids":["sec07-F19","sec07-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Quick right-on-red check","fact_ids":["sec07-F17","sec07-F16","sec07-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Turning right on red","fact_ids":["sec07-F17","sec07-F16","sec07-F15"]},{"text":"What comes first?","fact_ids":["sec07-F17","sec07-F16","sec07-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are at a steady red light and want to turn right, and no sign prohibits it. What must you do before turning? The answer is to stop before the crosswalk on the near side of the turn and yield to pedestrians lawfully in or next to it and to other traffic lawfully using the intersection. Right on red is allowed unless a sign prohibits it, but it always begins with that complete stop. Only after yielding to everyone with the right-of-way may you make the turn. Pedestrians in the crosswalk always come first. Treat every signal as an instruction, not a suggestion.","fact_ids":["sec07-F17","sec07-F16","sec07-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u02-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Traffic signals recap","fact_ids":["sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-F11","sec07-R03","sec07-F12","sec07-F13","sec07-R05","sec07-F14","sec07-F15","sec07-F16","sec07-F17","sec07-F18","sec07-R04","sec07-F19","sec07-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Green: go with caution","fact_ids":["sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-F11","sec07-R03","sec07-F12","sec07-F13","sec07-R05","sec07-F14","sec07-F15","sec07-F16","sec07-F17","sec07-F18","sec07-R04","sec07-F19","sec07-R06"]},{"text":"Yellow: steady stops, flashing slows","fact_ids":["sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-F11","sec07-R03","sec07-F12","sec07-F13","sec07-R05","sec07-F14","sec07-F15","sec07-F16","sec07-F17","sec07-F18","sec07-R04","sec07-F19","sec07-R06"]},{"text":"Red: steady waits, flashing works like a stop sign","fact_ids":["sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-F11","sec07-R03","sec07-F12","sec07-F13","sec07-R05","sec07-F14","sec07-F15","sec07-F16","sec07-F17","sec07-F18","sec07-R04","sec07-F19","sec07-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close, signals usually stack red over yellow over green, or run red, yellow, green from left to right, and some show a single color. Green means go with caution if clear. A steady yellow means stop and wait, unless you are already in the intersection, while a flashing yellow means slow down and proceed carefully. A steady red means wait for green, with right on red allowed after a full stop and yielding unless a sign forbids it, and a flashing red works like a stop sign. Allow for other drivers' mistakes at every light. When a signal confuses you, slow down and look carefully.","fact_ids":["sec07-F09","sec07-F10","sec07-F11","sec07-R03","sec07-F12","sec07-F13","sec07-R05","sec07-F14","sec07-F15","sec07-F16","sec07-F17","sec07-F18","sec07-R04","sec07-F19","sec07-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec07-u03","module_id":"sec07-m03","objective_ids":["sec07-u03"],"title":{"text":"Warning signs","fact_ids":["sec07-F20","sec07-R07","sec07-F21"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Warning signs give you time to prepare for danger before you reach it.","fact_ids":["sec07-F21"]},{"text":"Their yellow diamond shape, or fluorescent yellow near schools and crossings, lets you recognize them at a glance.","fact_ids":["sec07-F22","sec07-F20","sec07-F23"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Kim sees a yellow diamond sign warning of a sharp curve ahead on a rural road.","fact_ids":["sec07-F22","sec07-F26"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Warning signs tell you about possible danger ahead, such as a need to slow down and be ready to stop.","fact_ids":["sec07-F21"]},"result":{"text":"Kim slows before the curve, ready for whatever the sign warned about.","fact_ids":["sec07-F21"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking the manual's sign pages show every sign you will meet.","fact_ids":["sec07-R07"]},"correction":{"text":"The manual highlights only a selection of signs of interest to drivers and says it does not cover every sign.","fact_ids":["sec07-R07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Yellow diamond means danger ahead; brighter yellow means schools and walkers.","fact_ids":["sec07-F22","sec07-F23"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Which kinds of warning signs can appear in fluorescent yellow?","fact_ids":["sec07-F23"]},"answer":{"text":"Those for school zones, school crossings and pedestrian crossings.","fact_ids":["sec07-F23"]},"rationale":{"text":"The brighter fluorescent yellow draws extra attention to school and pedestrian areas.","fact_ids":["sec07-F23"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec07-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Signs that warn","fact_ids":["sec07-F20","sec07-F21","sec07-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Shape and color give clues","fact_ids":["sec07-F20","sec07-F21","sec07-R07"]},{"text":"Warning signs mean danger ahead","fact_ids":["sec07-F20","sec07-F21","sec07-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Traffic signs give information on traffic rules, hazards, location, directions and roadway services, and their shape, color, symbols and words hint at the kind of message they carry. Warning signs are the ones that tell you about possible danger ahead. In this unit you will learn what warning signs do, how most of them look, which ones may be fluorescent yellow, and the kinds of warning signs the manual includes. The manual highlights only a selection of signs of interest to drivers and says plainly that it does not cover every sign. Spotting a warning sign early gives you time to react calmly.","fact_ids":["sec07-F20","sec07-F21","sec07-R07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"What warning signs do","fact_ids":["sec07-F21","sec07-F22","sec07-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Danger ahead","fact_ids":["sec07-F21","sec07-F22","sec07-F23"]},{"text":"Slow down, be ready to stop","fact_ids":["sec07-F21","sec07-F22","sec07-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"Warning signs tell you about possible danger ahead, such as a need to slow down and be ready to stop, or a hazard or special situation on the road. They give you time to adjust before you reach the problem, whether it is a sharp curve, a merging lane or a crossing. Most warning signs are diamond shaped and colored yellow, with their lettering or symbols in black. Some, including those for school zones, school crossings and pedestrian crossings, may be fluorescent yellow to stand out even more. A quick glance at the sign's shape and color tells you a lot.","fact_ids":["sec07-F21","sec07-F22","sec07-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec07-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Road layout warnings","fact_ids":["sec07-F24","sec07-F25"]},"lines":[{"text":"Curves and curvy roads","fact_ids":["sec07-F24","sec07-F25"]},{"text":"Cross, side, T and Y intersections","fact_ids":["sec07-F24","sec07-F25"]}],"narration":{"text":"The manual's common warning signs include several that describe the shape of the road ahead. Among them are Right Curve and Curvy Road Ahead, which warn you to slow for bends, and Cross Road Ahead, Side Road Ahead, T-Intersection Ahead and Y-Intersection Ahead, which warn of roads joining yours. Further signs cover lanes and highways: Divided Highway Begins, Divided Highway Ends, Lane Ends, Merging Traffic, Added Lane and Traffic Signal Ahead.
